Techniques Used: Admissible branched coverings of labeled graphs
Data & Platforms: Fundamental Groups of Closed Orientable Surfaces
Application Areas: Classification and structural analysis of finitely presented groups and their splittings
Topological classification and volume minimization of hyperbolic 3-manifolds
Computation of geometric invariants such as stable commutator length in surface groups
Spectral theory and topological analysis of self-adjoint operators and canonical systems
Key Research Thinking Patterns: Bounded Complexity via Deformation Spaces: Establishing uniform bounds on the combinatorial complexity of group actions by analyzing the partial ordering of deformation spaces of G-trees (e.g., proving accessibility theorems for finite-index splittings of almost finitely presented groups using collapse maps and folds).

Combinatorial Encoding of Geometric Invariants: Translating continuous geometric problems into discrete combinatorial or linear algebraic frameworks to prove rationality and computability (e.g., encoding taut admissible surfaces as integer vectors to reduce stable commutator length computation to linear programming over rational polyhedra).

Invariant-Based Classification of Lattices: Distinguishing isomorphic or commensurable structures by constructing new algebraic or topological invariants that capture subtle structural differences (e.g., introducing the 'depth profile' invariant to distinguish incommensurable uniform lattices in the automorphism groups of Baumslag-Solitar complexes).

Group Action Topology for Operator Spaces: Utilizing the action of Lie groups on parameter spaces to determine the global topological structure of operator classes (e.g., analyzing the PSL(2, R) action on spaces of reflectionless canonical systems to prove homeomorphism to products of disks and tori).
Summary Description: Max Forester is a mathematician specializing in geometric group theory, low-dimensional topology, and spectral theory. His research focuses on the structural classification of finitely presented groups, particularly through the analysis of their actions on trees and splittings. He employs combinatorial and geometric methods to bound the complexity of group actions and classify uniform lattices in locally compact groups. In topology, he investigates hyperbolic 3-manifolds, focusing on volume minimization and the classification of manifolds with geodesic boundaries. Additionally, he applies combinatorial encoding techniques to compute geometric invariants like stable commutator length in surface groups. His work also extends to spectral theory, where he analyzes the topological properties of spaces of self-adjoint operators and canonical systems using group action theory. Forester's contributions provide rigorous frameworks for understanding the interplay between algebraic structure, geometric topology, and operator theory.
